title: Zakariyya's du'a
hook: don't leave me alone, You are the best of inheritors (21:89)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yunus in the dark, and your line, I was wrong. Today, an old man in a quiet room, asking for what looks impossible.

A sanctuary, a prayer chamber the Qur'an calls the mihrab. An old prophet named Zakariyya, the one the Bible calls Zechariah, is the guardian of a girl dedicated to God: Maryam. Surah three says that whenever he went in to her, he found food beside her that he hadn't brought. Where does this come from, he asks. From Allah, she says. And right there, the verse says, Zakariyya prayed. His hair is white. His wife has never had a child. He has no one to carry on after him. Watching that girl, he asks anyway.

The Qur'an tells his prayer more than once. Surah nineteen says he called in secret: my bones have grown weak, my head is shining with gray. Surah twenty-one gives it in one line. In Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Leave me not childless, though Thou art the best of inheritors." Pickthall writes childless, and that is the sense. But the Arabic word is fardan: alone, single, one by himself. So the plea underneath is today's line: don't leave me alone. Then the second half, easy to hear past. You are the best of inheritors. Everything a person leaves behind, a name, a house, a life's work, ends up with someone. Zakariyya says the One who finally inherits everything is Allah. Commentators have read that half as trust: if a son does not come, what I am is still not lost. So the prayer holds two things at once. He asks plainly for what he wants, and says ahead of time that he won't be abandoned even if the answer is no. The next verse says the answer was yes. Allah heard him, gave him Yahya, John, and made his wife able to bear a child. Then a detail about the whole family: they hurried to do good, and called on Allah in longing and in awe. Lonely people are not rare in this book. Yunus in the fish. Ayyub in his sickness. Zakariyya in an empty house. Each of them speaks, and each is heard.
screen: `MY BONES ARE WEAK, MY HEAD IS GRAY.`
`HEARD: YAHYA, AND A FAMILY THAT HURRIED.`

segments.voice: Bring one person to mind who is more alone than they let on, an older neighbor, a friend far from home, someone newly widowed, and picture where they are right now. If you pray, ask for them in your own words, or borrow Zakariyya's: don't leave them alone. If you don't, keep them company in your mind for the length of the sit.

Zakariyya's du'a. Don't leave me alone; You are the best of inheritors. This week ran from the garden's greeting of peace to Adam, Ibrahim, Musa, Ayyub, Yunus and Zakariyya: prophets, each praying in his own trouble. Today's word.
Your line: don't leave me alone. He asked plainly, and trusted either way. Day six hundred ninety-three, and counting.

howItsDone: Some couples hoping for a child recite Zakariyya's du'a from 21:89 and 3:38, and some Muslims also say its plea not to be left alone in times of loneliness.

original.note: Arabic: alone, single. Zakariyya asks not to be left fardan (21:89).

trapdoor: what you thought: an old man asking for a son.
what it means: don't leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors: ask plainly, and trust that nothing is lost.
what a scholar hears: Pickthall renders fardan as childless, but the word means single, alone, so the plea is wider than an heir.
recall: keep me praying, and accept my prayer

chat.says: Zakariyya was old and had no child. What did he ask for?
options: Don't leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors either way.
To make Maryam his heir, since he had raised her in the sanctuary.
Nothing; he accepted his age and never asked for a child.
chat.meaning: 21:89: Leave me not childless, though Thou art the best of inheritors. Fardan means alone; he asks plainly, and trusts either way.

Yahya.meaning: Zakariyya's son, known in English as John

Maryam.meaning: Mary, the girl in Zakariyya's care
